questions.question: When sorting with natural ordering, what does it mean if `s1.compareTo(s2)` returns a negative number?
options: s1 should come before s2
s1 should come after s2
s1 and s2 are equal and one of them will be removed
The comparison failed and the sort must stop
questions.explanation: The contract is: negative → s1 comes before s2, positive → s1 comes after s2, zero → they are considered equal in ordering. With `this.marks - other.marks`, a student with 10 marks compared to one with 20 gives -10, so the 10-mark student comes first (ascending). A negative value is a normal answer, not an error.

questions.question: `Collections.sort(names)` works on a `List<String>` and `Collections.sort(nums)` on a `List<Integer>`, but `Collections.sort(students)` on a `List<Student>` does not compile. What must you do so that students can be sorted by their natural order?
options: Override `equals()` in Student so that the sort can compare students
Override `toString()` so that students are sorted alphabetically by their text
Convert the list into an array first, because `Collections.sort` only accepts built-in types
Make Student implement `Comparable<Student>` and define `compareTo(Student other)`
questions.explanation: String and the wrapper classes already implement `Comparable`, so Java knows how to order them. For a custom class you must provide the contract "I know how to compare myself with another object of my type" by implementing `Comparable<Student>`. `equals` only says equal or not — it cannot say which object comes first.

questions.question: `Student.compareTo` sorts by marks ascending and, when marks are equal, by name. In what order are the students printed?
options: Aditya, Rohit, Monu, Rohan
Rohan, Monu, Rohit, Aditya
Rohan, Rohit, Monu, Aditya
Aditya, Monu, Rohan, Rohit
questions.explanation: `this.marks - other.marks` gives ascending marks: 56, 85, 85, 95. Rohit and Monu tie on 85, so the name comparison decides: "Monu" comes before "Rohit" lexicographically. The "Rohan, Rohit, Monu" option ignores the tie-breaker and keeps insertion order for equal marks.

questions.question: You want `Collections.sort(list)` to put the student with the HIGHEST marks first. Which `compareTo` body does that?
options: `return this.marks - other.marks;`
`return this.marks > other.marks ? 1 : 0;`
`return other.marks - this.marks;`
`return Math.abs(this.marks - other.marks);`
questions.explanation: With `other.marks - this.marks`, a student with 20 compared to one with 10 gives 10 - 20 = -10 (negative), so the 20-mark student comes first — descending order, as the lecture works through. `this.marks - other.marks` is ascending. The `? 1 : 0` version and `Math.abs` never return a negative value, so they break the contract (they can never say "this comes before other").

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: After sorting, the list is [1, 3, 3, 5, 8] and `binarySearch` finds 5 at index 3 (the search happens before the reverse, so the index refers to the sorted list). `reverse` then modifies the list in place to [8, 5, 3, 3, 1]. `frequency(list, 3)` counts 2 occurrences and `max` uses natural ordering, so it is 8 regardless of position.

questions.question: A teammate calls `Collections.binarySearch(list, 42)` on a list of IDs that were added in arrival order (never sorted). Sometimes it returns a negative number even though 42 is in the list. What is wrong?
options: `binarySearch` only works on a LinkedList, not on an ArrayList
`binarySearch` requires the list to be sorted first; on an unsorted list its result is undefined
`binarySearch` returns the count of matches, and a negative count means a duplicate was found
`binarySearch` always searches from the end, so it misses elements near the front
questions.explanation: Binary search achieves O(log n) by repeatedly halving the range, which only works if the data is ordered; on an unsorted list it can discard the half that contains the key. Sort the list (e.g. `Collections.sort`) first, or use a linear `contains`/`indexOf`. A negative return normally means "not found", not a count.

questions.question: The admin screen must list students sorted by marks, while the attendance screen must list the same students sorted by name. Why is Comparable alone not enough here?
options: Because Comparable can only be implemented by String and wrapper classes
Because `compareTo` can only compare int fields, not Strings
Because a class that implements Comparable can no longer be stored in a List
Because a class has exactly one `compareTo`, i.e. one natural ordering; other orderings need a separate Comparator
questions.explanation: Comparable bakes a single natural ordering into the class (one class → one natural ordering), so you cannot have both "by marks" and "by name" as `compareTo`. The lecture's answer for additional or non-obvious orderings is the `Comparator` interface, covered next. `compareTo` can compare any fields, including Strings via `name.compareTo(...)`.

questions.question: This `Student.compareTo` compares ONLY marks (no name tie-breaker). What does the program print?
options: 3 Monu false
2 Monu false
2 Monu true
3 Monu true
questions.explanation: TreeSet decides duplicates with `compareTo`, not `equals`: Rohit vs Aditya returns 0, so Rohit is treated as a duplicate and not added — size 2, and Monu (80) is the smallest. `contains` also uses `compareTo`, so a brand-new "Zara" with 95 compares as 0 with Aditya and the answer is true. This is the lecture's "danger of returning 0": if `a.compareTo(b) == 0`, make sure `a.equals(b)` is true too (Demo2 adds a name tie-breaker for this reason).

questions.question: A class keeps a private `ArrayList<String> items` and exposes `getItems()` returning `Collections.unmodifiableList(items)`. Which statement is correct?
options: It returns an independent copy, so later changes to `items` are not visible to callers
It returns a read-only view: callers' `add`/`remove` throw UnsupportedOperationException, but later changes the class makes to `items` are visible through the view
It makes `items` itself immutable, so the owning class can no longer add elements either
It silently ignores `add`/`remove` calls made on the returned list
questions.explanation: `unmodifiableList` wraps the original list in a read-only view: any modifying call through the wrapper throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, but reads go straight to the backing list, so the owner's later changes show up. It is not a snapshot copy (that would be `List.copyOf` or `new ArrayList<>(items)`), and it does not lock the original list.

questions.question: `Account.compareTo` returns `this.balance - other.balance` (int balances). Sorting works in tests, but in production, with balances like 2,000,000,000 and -2,000,000,000, some accounts come out in the wrong order. What is the cause and fix?
options: `Collections.sort` is unstable for large numbers; switch to a TreeSet
Negative numbers are not allowed in `compareTo`; store balances as absolute values
The list must be shuffled before sorting to avoid worst-case input
The subtraction overflows int and flips the sign; use `Integer.compare(this.balance, other.balance)`
questions.explanation: 2,000,000,000 - (-2,000,000,000) = 4,000,000,000 does not fit in an int, wraps around to a negative value, and tells the sort that the larger balance is smaller. The subtraction idiom from the lecture is fine for small ranges like marks, but `Integer.compare` returns the correct sign for any ints. Negative return values are a normal part of the contract, and a TreeSet would use the same broken `compareTo`.
